title: Do not define justifying faith by the consequent persuasion — or by refuge alone
source_text: LXXXVII. Sed tamen incommode & imperfecte fidem justificantem definiunt, qui dicunt illam esse certam persuasionem de Dei erga nos benevolentia & misericordia, & quod bona Evangelio promissa ad nos pertineant. Nec enim ista persuasio est actus quo justificamur, sed qui justificationem jam factam consequitur; & sine illo fides, saltem infirma, potest ad tempus subsistere. Jam autem est contra rationem, ut fides justificans describatur ab eo actu qui justificationem jam factam praesupponit, potius quam ab eo per quem justificamur; imo a tali actu sine quo fides consistere potest, & a quo potest separari: Adde quod est etiam a ratione alienum fidem justificantem ab unico actu describere, cum tamen ad eam concurrant alii actus eo non minus necessarii. Contra quod peccant illi quoque qui in fide definienda mentionem faciunt solius istius fiduciae per quam ad Deum confugimus, & gratiam ab eo quaerimus & expectamus.
pass_a_gloss: But yet they define justifying faith inconveniently and imperfectly who say that it is a certain persuasion of God's goodwill and mercy toward us, and that the goods promised in the Gospel pertain to us. For neither is that persuasion the act by which we are justified, but that which follows justification already made; and without it faith, at least weak faith, can for a time subsist. Now it is against reason that justifying faith be described from that act which presupposes justification already made, rather than from that through which we are justified; nay from such an act without which faith can stand, and from which it can be separated: Add that it is also foreign to reason to describe justifying faith from a single act, when yet other acts no less necessary concur to it. Against which those also offend who in defining faith make mention only of that trust by which we flee to God and seek and expect grace from him.
pass_b_english: Ill-formed: defining justifying faith as sure persuasion that God’s goodwill and Gospel goods are ours.
That persuasion follows justification already done; weak faith can briefly stand without it.
Unreasonable to define justifying faith by an act that presupposes justification — and can be parted from faith — rather than by the act through which we are justified.
Also unreasonable to pin the definition on one act when several necessary acts concur — including those who mention only refuge-fiducia fleeing to God for grace.
